Program: a recipe. Process: the cooking.
Program = the recipesteps written down; by itself it does nothing
baking #1step 1 of 8
baking #2step 1 of 8
Process = one baking, in progressits own step, its own bowl
One recipe, two bakings at onceone program, many processes

A process is a running program: the code plus where it is right now

    int buf_len;};

One call, two returns

    

      
1▶▶int main() {

      
2▶▶  printf("hello world (pid:%d)\n", getpid());

      
3▶▶  int rc = fork();

      
4▶▶  if (rc < 0) {

      
5▶▶    exit(1);                // fork failed

      
6▶▶  } else if (rc == 0) {

      
7▶▶    printf("hello, I am child (pid:%d)\n", getpid());

      
8▶▶  } else {

      
9▶▶    printf("hello, I am parent of %d (pid:%d)\n",

      
▶▶           rc, getpid());

      
10▶▶  }

      
11▶▶}

    

    
$ ./p1

    
29146parent

    
29147child

    
rc = 29147

    
rc = 0

Parent or child: who prints first?

    
    
I am parent

    
I am child

    
run 1

    
int rc_wait = wait(NULL);

    
Either order can happenthe scheduler decides who runs first

    
wait(): the parent sleeps until a child exitsnow the child always prints first; wait() returns the child's PID

    
After OSTEP Figure 5.2, p2.c (Arpaci-Dusseau) · wait(2)

    
Without wait(), the scheduler picks the order; wait() makes it certain

Pipe it into wc -l, and you get 8. Why?

    

    
terminal
$ ./a.out | wc -l
8

    
stdout is a terminal: printf writes out at every \n

    
stdout is a pipe: printf fills a buffer, written when full or at exit

    
    

    
pipe

    
0wc -l

    
fork() copies the buffer too

    

    
fork() copies unflushed output too, so flush before you forkfflush(stdout), setbuf(stdout, NULL), or stdbuf -oL

    
After Yanyan Jiang, fork-demo · setbuf(3), stdbuf(1)

1234parent

    
1235child

    
1systemd

status 0

ps

    
The child exitsthe kernel keeps its PID, status, and usage

Parent gone? PID 1 adopts itand waits for it automatically
